idiom_name: coroutine-context confinement: single-threaded dispatcher / limitedParallelism(1) / ThreadLocal.asContextElement()
implementation_notes: Kotlin has no thread-local syntax; on the JVM it inherits `ThreadLocal`, but coroutines are not bound to a thread, so the idiomatic realization is confinement to a coroutine context: run the state's operations on a single-threaded dispatcher (`Dispatchers.Main`, `newSingleThreadContext`, or `Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1)`) so accesses execute sequentially, or keep the state inside one coroutine and communicate through channels - kotlinlang.org documents this as 'thread confinement' and shows exactly these single-threaded-context forms. `ThreadLocal.asContextElement()` carries a JVM thread-local value across dispatcher hops so MDC/transaction-style libraries keep working under suspension, with the documented limitation that mutations inside the coroutine are not propagated back to the caller. The classic Java form (a ThreadLocal per OS thread) is still justified for genuinely thread-affine state such as JNI handles.
pitfalls: limitedParallelism(1) serializes execution but does not pin a thread: leaking state out of the confined section reintroduces races, and the backing thread may change between resumptions.
Reading a ThreadLocal from a coroutine without the matching context element yields undefined values, and in-coroutine mutations are lost on the next suspension (documented for asContextElement).
newSingleThreadContext owns a real thread that must be closed; prefer limitedParallelism(1) when only parallelism needs limiting.
